comments.body:
Man, this one is really so sad 😢😟😢. RIP, Dolly, and job well done.

Going strictly on demographics, I wouldn't exactly be the “typical” country music fan, but Dolly was always the exception. She seemed to transcend country and appeal to damn near everyone. I so adored what I knew of this woman, and I never met her a day in my life.

I've watched so many of her interviews and such over the years, and I rewatched a lot of them within the last year or so after she had to cancel events for health reasons. Yeah, she was 80 and had health concerns, but to me, she outwardly seemed to be doing well enough to tamp down the whispers that she was at death's door, so I truly didn't think it would come to this, at least not yet.

And here we are 😔. My goodness. A sobering reminder that we will all walk that road one day. That's just how it is.

Well...Dolly, you've earned your rest. Sad for sure, but you made 80! And now, you have no more race to run. You always told us you prided yourself on being a workhorse, but at last, your work is done. RIP 💖🙏🏾🥀🕊.

comments.name: Former Children’s Book Publisher
comments.body:
In my capacity as publisher of a major children’s book group which supplied her Imagination Library, I had the opportunity to meet Dolly back in 2006.  On my way to Dollywood, I stopped to visit my dying grandfather, who mentioned that Dolly’s “Coat of Many Colors” was his favorite song.  As I left, knowing it was the last time I’d see him, he said “would you ask Dolly to pray for me?”  

The next day, as we chatted backstage prior to a brief concert at her Dollywood theater, I passed along my grandfather’s request.  Dolly immediately stopped all the chatter in the room and said “let’s all pray for our brother Edward.”  She then said a heartfelt prayer, gave me a hug and left the room to get ready to sing.  

I’ve become aware over the years of many, many acts of charity and kindness that Dolly performed - many more than have been made public.  She was very likely the most generous, well-meaning celebrity of our time.  And I can’t wait to read the full-life biography that someone is going write about her, which will go far beyond what she, herself, was willing to put on paper in her 1994 autobiography.  Only then will the public get to know just what a great soul she was.

There doesn't seem to be any reason to assume that the percentage of players with CTE iin the population of 638 players whose brains were not examined is any different than the percentage in the population whose brains were examined - which would lead one to conclude that the percentage for the entire population is much more like 90% than 25%.That's horrifying.

comments.name: Radwon
comments.body: As a physician that bases my decisions on scientific data and evidence this study seems deeply flawed. 878 NFL deaths 2016-21. Of those they received 235 brains to study, 215 of which showed CTE. Why? What made those families decide to donate? The logical answer would be behavioral issues that made family members suspect of CTE. Perhaps not but this is a clear example of selection bias, that is, those studied are not representative of the population intended for research. And what of the 643 brains not donated for study. Again, why? Normal behavior prior to death, family not wanting to know, socioeconomic issues? Unanswered. The 24.5% rate is the floor. Is it possibly as high as 91% (215/235).

Controlling AI is obviously going to be very complex to implement. To reduce the complexity maybe the way to tackle the AI in our lives will be to tackle the implementation is simple/small steps. Teaching and adoption of ethics may be the highest order, but it is a hard sell for those with vacant ethical attitudes.
Options:
Real-time oral and/or paper exams in school - phones collected at the classroom door.  It is labor-intensive, but more comprehensive examinations can be reserved for proctored  credentialed exams. Anyone over 45 grew up with paper.  Ethics were endemic to the process.
For online programs that allow open book exams, even specialized essays are difficult to scrutinize for AI input. Peer pressure can be helpful.  Strong boundaries - Buddy systems - "Anyone caught posting AI-generated answers will automatically lose a letter grade for everyone in your buddy group."  This may be harsh and draconian, but the pressure point that "my cheating causes harm to others" is communicated and ultimately, the leverage sought to self-regulate. Unfair, but so is life! ;)
I teach in an online program and see AI slipping into the online posts.  If you open the classroom door at all to AI/ChatGPT, the slope is slippery, and almost unbearably difficult to avoid for tech-era students.  
I do agree in theory with the author.

In teaching about honesty, I made the point that once trust is broken, it is not only partially broken: For one might then become suspicious about lots of things regarding that person. In effect, then, it seems completely broken, for how and when can you trust that person again? One might never know for sure. I asked my students if I had ever lied to them, and they said no. They had always trusted me. But to my strong surprise, one student began to say that they were right now changing their mind. It was a student I never would have suspected of cheating or lying. But now, the student was saying, they are going to stick with integrity. It was in the last 10 minutes of class. I was, of course, so surprised that at some point that this particular student had cheated before, but was also so surprised that my little talk had been that effective. A lifetime of someone being honest, from my teaching, is a great reward to me--but also now to anyone who deals with that person--always.

Any occupation that had such rates of injury, especially to the brain, would be investigated and brought before Congress.  Politicians and lobbyists would be lining up to sponsor a bill to help the everyday worker.

But football is different; nothing to see here.  Except the billions of dollars it generates and the rich get richer.  

I love this game and played it for 45 years, albeit tackle football ended in college.  My teenage daughter asked just the other day if I had a son, would I let him play football, and if so, at what age.  It was a difficult question to answer, as football has been my sport, and I love it.  I told her no tackle football until high school at the earliest, if at all.

These are modern day gladiators, who are bigger, faster and stronger, generating an amazing amount of energy on each snap of the ball.  Jason Kelce once said “It’s a car wreck in every play.”

It’s time for the NFL, and government, to step up and not have a blind eye to the data and reality of the game and correlation to CTE.

Which is of course ridiculous, even if the brains they're testing are biased, some of the other brains must have CTE.  If you assume that the tested brains are 3 times as likely to have CTE, that would get you 46.5% of players have CTE.  And that's a big assumption, I would be willing to bet it's less than 3 times.  And of course even at 27%, it's clear football is worse than coal mining, it's worse than smoking, it's MUCH worse than drinking.  So forget about regulating what adults do, why are children allowed to play?  There's not much we could do about the adults, other than force the NFL to be touch football.

The loudest voices among us apparently hate doing things for others and thus hate the notion of a mutually supportive collective. We hate our government bureaucracy, but we also hate a socialist order.  There are those who love the notion of being independent and predatory.  The one thing the monarchy did for the other nations was to inspire folks to believe that their kings and queens owned a very limited, overly exploited patch of land that had been divided and doled out to royalty, while landless "people" were viewed as paupers. In America, land appeared early on to be up for grabs that strong white men could exploit. Else where monarchs alone had the option to dispense charity.  Their generosity was severely circumscribed however.  In America, each individual wished to have such largess and hate the "government" for taking this privilege away from them. They are as grasping and greedy as any royalty.  As such, they freakishly (or humanly) refuse to recognize that each voting and tax-paying American is the government. So, they give lip service to our republican democracy--one that has prevented the rise of land-grabbing monarchs.  Perversely, Americans claim to hate their safety net, coming up with all sorts of reasons why they hate and wish to have nothing to do with the government.   This confusing sentiment is as perverse as the belief of folks who still think the earth is flat.

I also wonder why no one talks about the extreme fluctuation in hormones that happens after birth. I had the baby blues with my first two, it did not last but menopause and ADHD ten years ago temporarily caused me to lose touch with reality. Turns out I was so thin at the time, I had zero detectable hormones, no sleep and serotonin syndrome from Prozac (I was not homicidal), and that will do it. In my case, estrogen, got me back to normal with CBT. Ms. Clancy is very thin, if she has any type of bipolar disease and was given a SSRI and was unable to sleep, it is no wonder she lost her mind. I played American football in high school and college. In those days when you tackled, blocked or ran the ball into anyone the coaches yelled, “Stick your head in there!” 

You were taught to lead with your head on both sides of the ball. Period. The more violent the hits the better. 

I also played soccer, the original football. In grade school I had to live in Liverpool for a few years with relatives because my mother died and my dad had to work so off we went from Boston to Merseyside. I learnt that game there. 

When I got out of college I went back and played some club football (soccer) over there in the lower divisions. Outside of heading the ball when needed you weren’t getting your skull banged on every play. It was rough but not a meat grinder. 

Parents, if you have a choice get your kids into the original football (soccer) because you only get one brain. If I had to do it over again I would never have played American football.  

I made good friends playing that game but what has stuck with me are not those friends, who are scattered to the wind or no longer with us, but my bent joints and three times broken nose, amongst other ailments. Those include years of bad headaches that come and go for no apparent reason and are a harsh reminder of my playing days. 

It’s up to families to make these decisions. American football isn’t going away regardless. It’s too ingrained to end. 

But it can help end a person too soon.

The token tax is an interesting idea, but ultimately flawed.  It's essentially a use tax which will both encourage "bootlegging" and will disproportionately impact consumers rather than producers.  As such, it will not--as Gates is encouraging --slow the transition process.

Because AI has such huge potential to radically inrease wealth inequality, AI needs to be taxed where the money lands rather than where it is spent, e.g. as a wealth tax.  On his blog, Gates starts to address this with a call to balance out the taxation of labor and capital.

Two things almost nobody is talking about are 1.) the phenomenon of Fordism going into an unrecoverable nose dive e.g. a consumer demand death spiral and 2.) the accelerated demise of all payroll tax funded government programs (SS, Medicare, Medicaid) which will happen on an accelerated timescale thanks to AI.

And, just in case some people are out there are still huffing Reaganesque "trickle down economics" fumes, that lie just got way bigger.

We're about to give a bunch of Tech Bros Archimedean levers.  Either--as Gates is hoping--we're going to figure this out in a human-centric way or those levers of power are going to get scary long and some of them may not have people at the other end activating them.

There are some indications such as a bumpy plateau for American oil production (I mean oil that is fracked) that America has reached or is about to reach its final "peak oil" (after reaching its conventional oil peak in 1972).

The traditional theory of geological peak oil, which predicts that oil production will peak and decline due to the physical depletion of easily accessible reserves, is not that helpful because it turns out that when countries get close to peak oil they might "lose their minds" and start wars and take other desperate actions leading to something called "geopolitical peak oil", which is a sort of emergent game theoretic type of ongoing situation. The point is to prevent other countries from getting oil, if you cannot get it yourself. We actually see that situation in this case as America has been unsuccessful in obtaining Iran's oil but still tries to make sure that China cannot get it. 

Diesel shortages and price spikes are just part of this scene. Probably oil will never be like it was before: something we can just take for granted.

Much will always be made of her creative genius and her legacy in singing, songwriting, acting, philanthropy and business. I just hope that future explorations of her private, personal life and unparalleled professional achievements, will also delve deeply into the spiritual foundations on which they were built. She lived loving God and loving our neighbors as ourselves. Like Jesus, Dolly loved the little children of the world. Like Jesus, she fed the hungry, healed the sick, embraced the marginalized and never forgot the poor in the community from which she had come. She was a miracle worker. That big-hearted, beautiful, buxom blonde conveyed such a profound understanding of the humanity we all share and spread love and laughter so widely that her death has broken hearts and occasioned deep grief around the world. if God was indeed one of us, I suspect he walked among us for 80 years in the guise of Dolly Parton of Pigeon Forge, Tennessee. I left with a beautiful cow hide, and kindled imagination about what she did with that teeny-tiny spotted suit, on that exotic curvaceous body, onstage.  Self-deprecation and parody could not cover up such a tantalizing spectacle.

We loved her wit and songs and the way she dressed.  She was herself.  Her passing has pulled together people today in a way that is missing from our everyday lives, which is another way we grieve her.

We are left in the mire of nastiness in this country.  We lost some joy today, and it reminds us of past happier times, that there are good people in the world and how little joy we have during our daily struggles with corruption, lying, poverty and mass incompetence at our top levels of government. Mr. Abumrad,

I can completely understand how you are unable to relate to how Ms Parton was able to mine her past to endlessly communicate its hardships and charm in such a way that captured people's hearts because that was the  world of our ancestors, full of similar values and drive, who came and settled all over this country and endured and strived with tremendous courage and often in terrible poverty. 

It was raw but there was also a simplicity and innocence as they lived and worked and worried together and endured and shrugged off their hardships with music forged from it.

That is the memory of so many of us, still in touch with our past and how we came to be, that Dolly Parton will always speak to in rhyme and rhythm.

We came from Europe mostly and forged a nation and though that appears harsh now and some want to criticize, that was the way of the world then. Yet nothing can be said to deny the bravery and hope of our ancestors who looked forward into the unknown and left all they knew to face a wilderness and often lost their lives to the challenge.

Some, off in the Smokies sang off their troubles and the hunger pains in their stomachs.

Those are the feelings Dolly Parton captured dressed in tinsel and unapologetically letting her roots shine!

comments.body:
The houses are stunning. I'm heading to Red Hook this weekend and will pass by to see them in person because I like architecture, especially this style.

Marvels of architecture and engineering they may be and heck a tree was saved! What's not to like except the price tag, but quality costs. 

To weave this story as a win for a nature and the love of a tree? So romantic. Sounds like a fairy tale to me, or sales pitch.

Four rowhouses totally around 30-40,000 sq ft from what I read, replaced one 2,250 sq ft 1899 house in a sorry state on a very large, ramshackle, overgrown lot. This means that almost every square inch of the plot is now covered in structure, leaving an 18 sq ft driveway and 8 sq feet at the back of each house.

A tree was saved but the open space of the yard and garden were sacrificed in the name of square footage. A roof terrace, lovely as that is, doesn't equally replace what was lost.

Yeah, I know, I'm really fun at parties.

The real environmental win, if there is one, is the porous driveway, which will not only help water the tree but hopefully lessen run-off of rainwater in a neighborhood prone to flooding (and is of benefit to the houses as well).

If it were my 400K, I would have used that money to build houses with smaller footprints, bigger yards and a tree or maybe two in each yard, but I'm a dreamer, and a tree lover.

I got an early taste of work (which I enjoyed) and discipline, developed a fairly utilitarian view of my looks (which I still think is healthier than seeing it as a reflection of my value as a human being), and got used to rejection. Plus, my parents put aside my earnings for university, and it came in extremely useful then.

comments.name: Katy B.
So Cal Therapist
comments.body:
As a therapist in Southern CA, I work with many cults who were pursuing professional acting as children, some of whom “succeeded” at booking work. I’m really moved by Allison Pill’s writing here.  It echoes much of what I see young adult Clients reckon with - pain over the experiences pursuing professional acting as a kid “that I asked for.” No child, no teenager, can consent to the losses of integrity and agency, many implicit, that just the pursuit (not booking) of child acting guarantees. Often a client responds to this “But it was legal.” My response to this is “Legal is not enough. I’m relieved that your caregiver didn’t engage you for illegal activity. But when I think of what I hope and wish for in the lives of little ones I care for, and protect, ‘legal’ is an unacceptably low standard.”

It is so very telling - and moving - that adult child actors with children of their own don’t permit this for their kids who do act: Jason Bateman, Gwyneth Paltrow, Katie Holmes. Perhaps they, too, with Allison Pill’s call, are a key to change here.

Dolly was extraordinary in her outreach to others.    She was out there performing, but she also was there to read books to children, to speak out for the need to aid the people about her flooded Gatlinburg, TN home town and for the need to get vaccines in the time of Covid 19.

Dolly was genuinely-ungenuine.  She sought to create a means to free the star from being merely the star of the distance from others.    She engineered a self-mocking form of attitude which placed her fame to the side in its self-effacing nature.    She was quoted as having told Tony Dokoupol that she had her hair done, but how long it took she did not know as she was not there to time it.    She claimed that she knew that she was not a dumb blond as she knew she was neither dumb nor even a blond.

The wink of the eye for the sake of 'cutting herself down to size' made her more the seeming sincere human being who wanted to remove herself from the otherwise difficult interface of the proscenium which traps most people who live with fame.

If I value anything of the artist, it is the ability to try to reach out to others by cutting the sense of distance away and at least appearing to be the more the person and less the personality!

comments.name: Matt Cook
comments.body:
Alexander Von Humboldt was the first anckno environmental scientist. Von Humboldt was exploring South America in 1800. “After he saw the devastating environmental effects of colonial plantations at Lake Valencia in Venezuela in 1800, Humboldt became the first scientist to talk about harmful human-induced climate change… He warned that humans were meddling with the climate and that this could have an unforeseeable impact on ‘future generations.’” (P.5, “The invention of Nature: The Adventures of Alexander Von Humboldt The Lost Hero of Science.”)
Also from page 5 of Andrea Wulf’s excellent biography: “Charles Darwin wrote that ‘nothing ever stimulated my zeal so much as reading Humboldt’s Personal Narrative’ saying that he would not have boarded the Beagle, nor conceived of ‘The Origin of Species’ without Humboldt.” 

What directly followed Von Humboldt was the development of environmental science. The 1864 book, “Man and Nature,” by George Perkins Marsh is a deep and well documented work on all aspects of environmental research. Much significant work on environmentalism closely followed and constantly appeared in scientific research and public knowledge, up to this day.

There may be reasons why we have destroyed our own planet, but there is no excuse for our refusal to respond to the documented and demonstrated evidence of more than two centuries.
The “unforeseeable impact on future generations,” Humboldt warned about turns out to have been truly foreseen, long ago.

I played football from 10 years old through Division I college football as a running back. Suffered numerous concussions and other physical injuries and at 73, I have no regrets. Unfortunately there are some of my college team mates, that  very sadly, succumbed to CTE later in life.  There was risk then and more evident risk now. 

My point, there is long term risk with any contact sport and many long term benefits.  Now that CTE is a proven risk,  measures have been, are and will continue to be taken to mitigate such risk.  I did not encourage or discourage any of my four children from playing a contact sport, including football.   One of my three sons played football through high school, another played soccer (think headers) through college (both suffered concussions).  Both are now doing extremely well in life.  There was full disclosure to them as to known risks at the time, and each  made  their choice to live their life with whatever may come.  Knowing what i know today, I console my eight grandchildren, with parental approval, in the same manner. Consider the risks, make your choice, live YOUR life!

comments.name: Claire
comments.body: This is an unfortunate abuse of trust for vulnerable people desperate for a cure. Who among us Gen X and Boomers didn't grow up seeing someone carelessly take psychedelics without regard to their surroundings? It did not end well for many. These are not drugs to be taken without great care. It was my cardinal rule to trip in a specific environment with specific people. I feel sad these people didn't have the positive experience they sought and deserved.

comments.body: I have had treatments in the clinic and treatments at home. I have decided that I don't ever want someone at one of these clinics to have control over me in a vulnerable state. Also, the so-called wisdom that you need someone to guide you is unsupported. Let's return to using mind altering drugs at home.

comments.name: Sophia
comments.body: No offense but if you participate in psychedelic journeys, it’s up to you to do your own due diligence around safety, contraindications, and the organization or individual who’s offering the ceremony. A plethora of information is available through reputable websites. If those guidelines are followed, psychedelics can be safe. I’d also add that if you’re afraid, then psychedelics are probably not for you. Healthy respect is in order. Fear is an entirely different matter.

comments.name: Nicholas
comments.body: To straddle the middle - I would say this. Western therapy is not “one sized fits all” and while it can be helpful for certain things, it is often limited in enacting real change in regards to depression, suicidal ideation, addiction and trauma. I recognize that may “sound” critical but the rates of mental health issues in the United States continue only to rise - and psychology as a discipline is really only 150 years old. I completely agree that there is danger with outsourcing ones help with traveling overseas but people are going to continue to do it until the US establishes clinics that follow safety guidelines. Many people including women - die in US hospitals ( that have plenty of safety guidelines ) especially during childbirth but is that ever reported on? I’m just using that as an example to illustrate that the thr US is not some paragon of health in comparison to other countries. People will continue to use psychedelics abroad, and likely will be harmed until the US implements its own system. I feel very lucky to have gone to Peru with Arkana and return to the US with a jungian depth psychologist to help me make sense of the incredible experience I had. Psychedelics are not for everyone, and most clinics with real doctors are thousands of dollars. I’d love if that money went to help raise awareness in the United States but it will take time.

comments.name: JS
comments.body: Are we forgetting that the people involved in these stories are legal adults and capable of making informed decisions, which involve risk/benefit analyses? And that there are plenty of horror stories within the medical establishment, including licensed doctors and clinicians who abuse their patients and insurance companies that neglect dying patients and deny them care? Americans, unless they're very wealthy and well connected, are without a paddle in the healthcare system. It's the wild west no matter which side of the aisle you're on - the Western medicine side, or the "Alternative" side. There's risk and precarity everywhere.

comments.name: Mari
comments.body:
I will say that low-dose ketamine did help me overcome depression/anxiety along with therapy (for the record: the meds they give you are not supposed to be longterm!) and I no longer need it.

I will also say that the cost of getting the better, more effective ketamine therapy in a doctor's office is incredibly high here and is not covered by insurance. I was quoted maybe $2k or $3k for a few sessions and they have done follow up calls for probably half a year now despite me telling them I'm not interested. 

I completely understand why people are willing to take the risk. In a certain headspace, it can feel like "I need to change or there is no hope."

comments.name: Clyde

comments.name: 430- Edward
comments.body:
Before judging the people seeking this kind of treatment, please understand that they are desperate for a change in their condition. 
That said, regarding treatment for addiction and alcoholism, in my experience, it might have taken twenty years to walk into those dark woods, but it’s only twelve steps to a better life. Just twelve steps. Try that, before you try any of these super risky “treatments.” 
Yes, it’s hard. It’s hard not to use. It’s hard to change. It’s hard but it gets easier. It doesn’t get easy. But, if you can be honest, open minded and willing, then you have a fighting chance. It works if you work it!

They aren’t just apps you can download and run to magically patch vulnerabilities in your banking software, or detect and block intrusions in your WiFi network.  It’s the web browser companies and the banks, payment systems, brokerages, that have to use various AIs to find the weaknesses in their systems and patch them. There is no way to stop or significantly regulate AI. There is only one technology where significant regulation has occurred, and that's atomic energy... because this requires fissile material that is relatively easy to detect and difficult to create. Anyone, anywhere, can develop malicious AI agents. You can't stop this.

Agents WILL attack systems, for example, financial systems, and agents WILL defend systems. Some attacks WILL succeed.

This cannot be prevented.

What we need is robust systems for backup and recovery so the damage done by attacks can be undone. That should be the focus.

If money disappears from my investment accounts, I want to be sure that my correct balances can be restored. That's what I care about. Otherwise, I will need to store gold under my mattress.

comments.name: Antoine
comments.body:
Fun fact: Irregular, the company whose CEO is quietly reassuring us in this article, is actually the company that couldn't handle the frontier llms that went rogue and attacked Hugging Face. Quite reassuring indeed, that the people who are among the best experts at AI security got outsmarted by 3 frontier llms recently, don't you think?
Fundamentally, this article is out of balance. No, it's not that some experts think this and others think the opposite. There is an obvious assymetry against defense that is going to make it impossible to secure applications.
- First, as some comment already mentioned, attackers need only succeed once. Defenders need 100% success, all the time.
- Second, it seems like some people expect AI to magically find all the vulnerabilities, and make our application secured once and for all. But there is and will be no such thing as perfect code. Therefore, defendants will always have to upgrade systems, which is incredibly costly. On the attackers side, all you have to do is retry with the next llm as soon as it gets released.
- Third, and that is possibly the most consequential, the most capable models are not able to find all the vulnerabilities that less capable models can find. Yes, you read it correctly, and that was actually in another recent times article. In a test, while frontier models find, and by far, more vulnerabilities, some were discovered solely by a less capable models. Good luck to defend against all the models in the world.

comments.body: This story is based on a mistaken assumption -- that Daniel J. Sullivan ("J") will inevitably act as a spoiler for Daniel S. Sullivan ("S"). One beauty of Alaska's unique electoral system is that ranked choice voting minimizes the chance that any candidate can act as a spoiler. The nonpartisan primary (a key Alaska innovation) has resulted in four candidates for the general election, including J and S. Ranked choice voting (another important Alaska election procedure) in the general election will determine the winner of the four candidates. J seems unlikely to rank in the top two candidates after first- and second-choice votes are tallied, so J supporters will have their second- or third-choice votes allocated among the remaining candidates, one of whom could indeed be S. In most other states, the spoiler problem is a serious drawback -- but not in Alaska's elections. Hopefully the attention drawn by J vs. S will help educate voters in other states about the incredible advantages of a single, nonpartisan primary that provides real choice (a field of four candidates) to voters in the general election, and provides an "instant runoff" feature in ranked choice voting that ensures the winning candidate in the general election receives a majority, and not just a plurality, of votes cast.

The causes of that earlier war and the fact that the Athenians did not follow Pericles' advice and he died of the plague before he could have any further influence on them, don't detract from the fact that nobody thought he was wrong to urge Athenians to remain free. And in America, we also didn't want to be part of another empire just as Athenians did not want to be Macedonians. It may be true that Athenians suffered under bad demogogues. This is a tragedy for the patient and her family and while there may be no single individual at fault, the administration of the wrong medication represents a system failure.  Medicine strives for a "zero failure" rate modeled after the airline and nuclear power industries, but all realize that humans are fallible so multiple checks are in place particularly in "high risk" environments.  Acute care hospitals represent a high risk environment, and ORs represent particularly high risk settings. In order to minimize errors, multiple checks are set in place to minimize "errors".  If the process was followed appropriately, this represents a process failure and a "root cause" analysis id undertaken to determine what safety gap needs to be filled.  However, if the process was not followed, then blame may shift to the "team" or to a single individual who chose to not follow the safety process. 
Add to this the fact that patients in hospital are sicker than in the past and more complex, specialized care is utilized in these patients all of which increases risk,  Additionally, the shortage of staff in hospitals (physicians, nurses, pharmacists, med techs, etc) has made hospitals even more dangerous. Hospitals generally run with small "profit" margins due to payments from insurers and the gov't not meeting the true cost of healthcare in this country. When on factors in the hours and stress on employees with (relatively) low wages, then the staff shortages are not surprising

My thoughts about pieces like this on education are simple: the record of academic (i.e. from unuversity eductaion departments) are so awful in the medium or long run that I discount anything like "studies" of or by their programs.  

I taught college for 43 years at a departmkent ranked #6 in the country. I found that the abilities of the students never changed over that period. About 50% had abysmal abilities, about 3% were brilliant, the others spread equally in between. The racial makeup did change (Asian up, everybody else down with their relative makeup unchanged). But interestingly I noticed one clear difference: over the years the number of students in the middle third  coming in for help, and those in the top 3% coming in to ask questions (usually "why"), not for help, rose a lot. That didn't happen for merely "good" or "bad" students. 

None of the methodologial changes they had experienced seem to have changed their abilities. I still therefore think that abilities are determined at conception, in the DNA. But this was a very technical subject.

Phoenicians, Greeks, and Romans were the foundational pillars that wove and formed Western civilization. Byblos was the main seat of the Phoenicians as they expanded their influence across the Mediterranean, reaching as far as the British Isles to trade for tin and exploring the Atlantic coast of Africa. They were the first civilization to build truly seaworthy boats, and the Phoenician alphabet serves as the basis for our modern script. In Vulgar and Medieval Latin, the phrase ‘ab oculis’ literally means ‘without eyes’ which evolved to ‘enveigle’ with the meaning shifting from physical blindness to blinding someone's judgment using clever tricks or charm.
